ctaTitle: Ready to Start Your Commercial Project?
ctaText: Let's walk through your project phase by phase. We'll tell you exactly what to expect, what to plan for, and how we'll communicate every step of the way.
content:
Nobody tells you what construction actually feels like.

The contractor talks about schedule, budget, and deliverables. The architect talks about design intent. And you — the owner — show up on day one of construction with a mix of excitement, anxiety, and a list of questions you're not sure are reasonable to ask.

This article is for you.

Not the contractor. Not the architect. You — the person whose money is being spent, whose business depends on the outcome, and who has never done this before or hasn't done it in a long time.

Here's what commercial construction actually looks like, phase by phase, in plain language. No jargon. No optimism that doesn't reflect reality. Just an honest account of what happens, what to expect, and what to do when things don't go exactly to plan.

Because they won't. And that's okay.

The best construction clients aren't the ones who never ask questions. They're the ones who ask the right questions — early enough to matter.

Before We Start: A Reality Check

Commercial construction is complex. It involves dozens of parties, thousands of decisions, and conditions that no one can fully predict before ground breaks.

Saying this is not an excuse. It's context.

Projects managed well still encounter unexpected site conditions, permit delays, material lead time surprises, and weather disruptions. The difference between a good project experience and a bad one is not whether these things happen. It's whether your contractor handles them professionally when they do.

What you should expect from a great contractor:

  • Proactive communication — you hear about problems from them, not because you asked
  • Options, not surprises — 'here's what happened, here are your choices, here's our recommendation'
  • Documentation — every issue and resolution in writing, no verbal-only conversations on important matters
  • Schedule transparency — weekly updates that show actual vs. planned progress, not just 'things are going well'
  • Budget integrity — no cost increase without a written change order you've approved

If your contractor is not providing these things — ask for them. Every professional contractor either has these systems or can implement them quickly. Resistance to basic project communication is a warning sign.

The Keentel Standard → We provide every client with weekly schedule reports, a dedicated project point of contact, and a documented change order process. Before we mobilize, you know exactly how we communicate and exactly what to expect from us.

The 8 Phases of Commercial Construction — What Actually Happens

Here's the complete picture. Every commercial project moves through these phases in roughly this sequence — with some overlap depending on project type and delivery method.

PhaseTypical DurationWhat You See
1. Pre-Construction4 – 16 weeksPlanning, design review, permitting, procurement
2. Site Preparation1 – 4 weeksClearing, grading, utility work begins
3. Foundation2 – 6 weeksConcrete poured, cured, inspected
4. Structural Work3 – 10 weeksSteel, framing — building takes shape
5. MEP Rough-In4 – 10 weeksPipes, conduit, ductwork inside walls
6. Insulation & Drywall3 – 8 weeksWalls close — spaces emerge
7. Finishes4 – 12 weeksFlooring, paint, ceilings, millwork, fixtures
8. Final Inspections & Closeout2 – 6 weeksInspections, punch list, certificate of occupancy

Now let's go deeper on each one — because knowing the name of a phase and knowing what it feels like are very different things.

Phase 1: Pre-Construction — The Slow Phase That Saves the Fast Ones

This phase feels like nothing is happening. That feeling is wrong.

Pre-construction is where your budget gets grounded in reality, your schedule gets built from actual task durations, and your design gets reviewed for constructability. It's where long-lead materials get ordered, subcontractors get lined up, and permit applications get submitted.

The projects that move fastest during construction are the ones where pre-construction was done most thoroughly. The projects that feel chaotic in the field are the ones that skipped it.

What you'll be doing during pre-construction: reviewing and approving design decisions, making material selections, signing off on the project schedule, and getting familiar with your contractor's communication process.

Don't rush this phase. The time you invest here comes back to you during construction.

Phase 2: Site Preparation — The Beginning of Visible Progress

This is when construction becomes real. Crews arrive. Equipment shows up. The site changes.

Site prep covers clearing and grubbing (removing vegetation and existing structures), grading the site to the right elevations, installing erosion control, and beginning underground utility work.

In Florida, this phase also often involves dewatering — managing groundwater during excavation — because the water table across much of the peninsula is shallow. A contractor experienced in Florida construction plans for this. An inexperienced one discovers it.

What you'll see: Heavy equipment. Dirt moving. Not much that looks like a building yet. That's normal.

Florida Note → If your site is in a flood zone, near wetlands, or in a coastal area, additional permits and environmental controls may be required during site preparation. Your contractor should have planned for this during pre-construction — but if it surprises them during site work, ask why.

Phase 3: Foundation — The Most Critical Work Nobody Sees

Foundation work is the most consequential phase in any construction project. It's also the one that looks the least impressive.

For most commercial projects in Florida, this means concrete footings, grade beams, and slab-on-grade. The soil conditions, water table, and building loads determine the foundation type.

This phase has mandatory inspection holds. The foundation cannot be covered until it's inspected and approved by the building department. These holds are not your contractor dragging their feet — they're legal requirements that protect your building.

What you'll see: Excavation. Rebar. Concrete being poured and then... waiting. Concrete cures, not dries. Curing takes time and the schedule accounts for it.

Patience Point → Foundation concrete typically requires 28 days to reach full design strength, though construction can often continue on it sooner. Don't interpret the curing period as inactivity — other site work continues in parallel.

Phase 4: Structural Work — The Phase Where It Starts Looking Like a Building

Steel erection or wood framing goes up. The building's skeleton becomes visible. This is typically the most visually exciting phase for owners.

For commercial buildings, structural steel is most common. For smaller commercial projects, light-gauge steel or wood frame may be used. The structural system was designed by the structural engineer and reviewed during pre-construction.

Progress feels fast during this phase. Crews are active, the structure grows daily, and for the first time you can walk through and understand the spaces.

What you'll see: Steel columns and beams. Roof deck. Exterior wall framing. The building's footprint and height become real.

Phase 5: MEP Rough-In — The Work That Lives in Your Walls Forever

Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing rough-in is the invisible infrastructure of your building. It goes in before the walls close and lives behind the drywall for the building's entire life.

This phase is where the most subcontractor coordination happens. Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing trades must sequence their work without conflict — pipes, conduit, and ductwork must coexist in the same ceiling cavities and wall spaces.

A good GC coordinates this through detailed MEP coordination drawings. A GC who doesn't coordinate this phase discovers the conflicts when two trades show up to occupy the same space on the same day.

Rough-in inspections are required before walls close. These are not optional delays — they're the process that ensures your building's infrastructure is code-compliant before it's permanently hidden.

What you'll see: Pipes, conduit, and ductwork running through open stud walls. The building looks more complex, not more finished. That's correct.

The MEP Reality → MEP systems represent 25–35% of total commercial construction cost. The rough-in phase is when that investment is made. A GC who is cutting corners on MEP coordination is cutting corners on the most critical and longest-lived infrastructure in your building.

Phase 6: Insulation and Drywall — The Transformation

This is the phase where the building transforms from a skeleton into something that looks like an interior space.

Insulation goes in — in walls, ceilings, and sometimes floors. Then drywall. Then taping, mudding, and sanding.

Progress during this phase can feel slower than it is. Drywall finishing requires multiple coats of compound with drying time between each. The sequence is correct. Rushing it shows in the final finish.

What you'll see: Spaces close in. Rooms become rooms. For the first time, you can walk through and feel what the finished building will be like.

What you'll also notice: Dust. Construction dust is a fact of life during this phase. On occupied renovations, dust mitigation is an active responsibility — ask your contractor what controls are in place.

Phase 7: Finishes — Where Quality Becomes Visible

Flooring. Paint. Ceiling systems. Millwork, cabinetry, and built-ins. Hardware, fixtures, and trim. MEP trim-out — the visible devices that connect to the rough-in infrastructure.

Finish work takes longer than most owners expect. Not because the work is slow. Because finish work has sequence dependencies — paint before flooring, millwork before paint, flooring before base trim. And because quality finish work takes the time it takes.

This is also the phase where the selections you made months ago become real. The flooring sample you approved looks different at full scale. The paint color you chose looks different under construction lighting than it will under finished lighting.

Take a breath. Most things look better when the project is complete and the lights are on.

Finish work is where your building goes from being a construction project to being your building. Give it the time it deserves.

Phase 8: Final Inspections and Closeout — The Last Mile

Final building inspections. Systems commissioning — HVAC tested and balanced, electrical systems verified, plumbing tested under pressure. The punch list. The Certificate of Occupancy.

The punch list deserves specific attention. A punch list is a documented list of incomplete or deficient items identified during a final walkthrough. It is not a sign that the project failed. It's a professional quality process that every well-managed project uses to ensure nothing is missed before handover.

What matters is not whether there's a punch list — there will always be one. What matters is how quickly and completely your contractor resolves it.

Closeout also includes: project documentation delivered to you, warranties assembled and provided, as-built drawings showing what was actually built, and any required operator training on building systems.

Certificate of Occupancy → The CO is issued by the building department after final inspections pass. In Florida, CO issuance typically takes 1–5 business days after final inspection approval, depending on the municipality. You cannot legally occupy a commercial building without a CO — so final inspections are a schedule-critical milestone.

Your Role as Owner — What Your Contractor Needs From You

The owner's performance during construction affects the project outcome more than most owners realize.

Here's what professional contractors need from their clients to deliver their best work:

What Your Contractor Needs From YouWhy It Matters
Prompt decisions on design and material selectionsEvery deferred decision delays work downstream — often by more than the decision itself took
Single point of contact on your teamMultiple voices giving different instructions create confusion and mistakes on site
Quick change order approvalsWork stops waiting for authorization — days of delay compound into weeks
Timely payment per the contract scheduleCash flow issues affect subcontractor performance and material procurement
Clear communication of operational constraintsYour contractor needs to know what's off-limits when, especially on occupied renovations
Trust the process — don't micromanage on-siteToo many cooks on a job site create confusion, contradict supervisors, and slow crews

None of these are burdens. They're the behaviors that consistently produce the best project experiences — for everyone.

The Surprises That Aren't Really Surprises

Every experienced construction owner knows these happen. First-timers are surprised. Here's how to be ready.

Hidden site conditions

Something unexpected is found below ground on almost every project that involves excavation. Underground utilities not shown on surveys. Old buried structures. Soil conditions that differ from the borings.

A professional contractor stops work, communicates immediately, presents options with pricing, and waits for your authorization before proceeding. No professional contractor surprises you with a change order after the fact for hidden conditions they discovered and resolved without telling you.

Permit revision requests

Plan examiners in Florida regularly come back with questions, clarifications, or required modifications to permit applications. This is normal. It is not your contractor's failure. What matters is how quickly they respond and whether they've planned for this possibility in your schedule.

Material lead time surprises

Specific products — custom millwork, specialty MEP equipment, particular flooring or tile — sometimes have longer lead times than anticipated. This is why procurement planning happens during pre-construction. If it happens anyway, your contractor should have identified it early and communicated options.

Weather in Florida

Summer afternoon storms are a fact of life in Florida from June through September. Tropical systems can affect schedules more significantly. A Florida contractor's schedule accounts for weather. If yours doesn't, ask why.

The Principle → A surprise that your contractor tells you about immediately and presents a solution for is not a project failure. A surprise you discover yourself — because your contractor didn't communicate — is a contractor failure. Know the difference.

Questions You Should Feel Free to Ask

There are no unreasonable questions when it's your project and your money.

  • 'Can I visit the site? What are the protocols?'
  • 'What's on the critical path right now and is it on track?'
  • 'What's the one thing most likely to affect our schedule in the next 30 days?'
  • 'Are there any pending decisions from me that are holding things up?'
  • 'When will the next inspection happen and what happens if it doesn't pass?'
  • 'What does the punch list process look like and when does it begin?'
  • 'What documentation will I receive at project closeout?'

A great contractor welcomes these questions. They're evidence of an engaged owner. Engaged owners make better decisions faster, which makes projects go better.

What the End Feels Like

There's a moment — usually toward the end of the finish phase — when the project stops looking like a construction site and starts looking like the building you imagined.

The floors are down. The paint is on. The lights work. You walk through and for the first time you see what all the months of planning, decisions, noise, and dust were building toward.

That moment is why we do this.

faqs.q: How often should I expect to hear from my general contractor during construction?
faqs.a: At minimum, weekly written progress reports showing actual vs. planned schedule, upcoming milestones, and any open items requiring your decision. More frequent updates during critical phases. Immediate contact for anything that affects schedule, budget, or safety. If you're not receiving this, ask for it — any professional contractor can provide it.

faqs.q: Can I visit the construction site during the project?
faqs.a: Yes, with coordination. Active construction sites have safety requirements — hard hat, hi-vis vest, closed-toe shoes, and escort by your project manager. Don't show up unannounced and don't direct workers directly. All direction goes through your contractor's project manager. Site visits are encouraged — seeing progress helps you stay informed and engaged.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a change order and a construction defect?
faqs.a: A change order is a documented modification to the original scope of work — something added, removed, or changed from the original contract. A construction defect is work that fails to meet the contractual standards for quality or specification. You pay for change orders. You don't pay for defect corrections — the contractor remedies those at their cost. Get both types of issues in writing.

faqs.q: What happens if my contractor misses a milestone?
faqs.a: The right response depends on why. Weather, permit delays, or hidden site conditions are legitimate causes that your contract should address with schedule extension provisions. Poor subcontractor management, inadequate planning, or labor shortages are contractor performance issues. Ask for a revised critical path schedule showing how they plan to recover, and what the new completion date is.

faqs.q: How long does the punch list process take?
faqs.a: For a well-managed project, the punch list walk typically takes 2–4 hours for a mid-size commercial build. Resolution of punch list items typically takes 2–4 weeks depending on the number of items and the availability of trades to complete them. A long punch list or slow resolution is a sign of inadequate quality control during construction.

faqs.q: What warranties should I receive at project completion?
faqs.a: You should receive: the general contractor's workmanship warranty (typically 1 year), subcontractor warranties, and all manufacturer warranties for major equipment and systems (HVAC, roofing, electrical equipment). Ask for a warranty binder at closeout — a well-organized contractor delivers this without being asked.
